aliases: Feng Huang Dancong Tuan Shu Ye
processing: As with other Dancong: withered, tossed for partial oxidation, fixed, rolled and dried over heat. Nothing specific to this strain is well documented.
harvest_season: Usually spring, as with most Fenghuang Dancong.
appearance_dry: Typically tight, straight, dark brown strips with an oily sheen, as is usual for the gardenia-aroma group.
appearance_liquor: Bright orange-yellow, typical of gardenia-aroma Dancong.
appearance_wet: Typically thick leaves with reddened edges, as with other tossed Dancong.
taste_profile: Listed among the strains with a natural gardenia aroma; the group usually gives a high floral nose, a mellow fresh body and a strong sweet return.

brewing.notes: Short steeps, as with any Dancong; long ones bring out bitterness.

vintage_note: As is usual for Dancong, it is sold by harvest year and season, mostly current-year spring tea, sometimes rested a year or two after roasting. It rarely appears under its own name, so ask the seller which tree or strain the leaf comes from.
description:
Tuan Shu Ye is a rarely seen Fenghuang Dancong strain from Guangdong, listed among the seven strains of the gardenia-aroma group that carry a natural gardenia scent.

Little is written about how this strain is handled. Expect standard Dancong work: withering, patient tossing to bruise the leaf edges, then fixing, rolling and drying with some roast.

The group's usual cup is high gardenia on the nose, a mellow fresh body and a clear sweet return. Brew it with plenty of leaf in a small gaiwan and pour off quickly.

The name itself needs care. Sellers and writers do not all mean the same thing by it, so a bag labelled Tuan Shu Ye may simply be gardenia-aroma tea from the wider Song Zhong family.
history: Little is documented about this strain on its own. Chinese accounts disagree: one lists Tuan Shu Ye as its own strain in the gardenia group, while others give it as an early name of the Song Zhong tree later called Da Ye Xiang and Huang Zhi Xiang. One tea seller's account says the name came from the shape of the leaf. Whether these all refer to one tree remains unclear.
